name: sdsl::bit_vector (SDSL - Succinct Data Structure Library)
claimed_speedup: Project's own description (SDSL 3.0 docs/wiki): sdsl::bit_vector is 'an optimized replacement of the infamous std::vector<bool>'. No numeric benchmark located for this specific claim within the research budget.
stars_or_usage: 2,309 stars; de facto standard succinct-data-structures library, extremely widely cited in the IR/bioinformatics/text-indexing literature (e.g. underlies the SPIRE 2014 sdsl-lite paper and dozens of downstream tools)
tradeoffs: bit_vector itself is a packed bit array similar in spirit to std::vector<bool> but without a standard-library iterator/allocator interface or thread-safety guarantees for concurrent bit writes; the library's real value is the rank/select/compressed layers built on top (rrr_vector, sd_vector, wt_*), which are not literal std::vector<bool>/std::bitset drop-ins and add their own space/time tradeoffs.
caveats: Could not confirm a specific numeric benchmark for bit_vector vs std::vector<bool> within the tool budget for this run; the 'optimized replacement' framing is a first-party claim with no accompanying numbers found, so this is Tier D. Included as this run's one allowed Tier-D entry because the project is unambiguously notable (2.3k stars, foundational in its field). Repository has not been pushed to since 2023-06-02 (>3 years), so maintenance_status is 'abandoned' despite the project's continued heavy citation/usage.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'succinct rank select bit vector github faster than std::vector<bool> C++' -> https://github.com/simongog/sdsl-lite

verification.tier_reason: benchmark_url is null, and no SDSL source compares sdsl::bit_vector against std::vector<bool>: not the README, the benchmark/ suite (FM-index, rrr_vector, wavelet trees, etc.), nor the SDSL arXiv paper 1311.1249. The only 'claim' is misattributed.
verification.notes: Rejected because the record's only evidence belongs to another project (bkille/BitLib, BSD-3-Clause, 76 stars, whose README has Google Benchmark results against std::vector<bool>; worth a separate candidate record). SDSL itself makes no speed claim against a stdlib baseline, though it is notable (2,309 stars). The last commit on default branch master is 2019-12-11; the 2023-06-02 date is the repo pushed_at (a non-default branch). The maintained SDSL v3 is the fork xxsds/sdsl-lite (110 stars), whose README also has no std::vector<bool> claim.

name: Collections-C CC_HashTable (also CC_List, CC_Deque, CC_TreeTable)
baseline: std::unordered_map<int, void*> (also std::map, std::list, std::deque; the same run also compares GNOME glib 2.63.0 GHashTable/GTree/GList/GQueue and cdcontainers)
workload: Google Benchmark loops of N = 4 to 122,880 random-int operations on containers holding void* values: map insert, remove and search by key, iterator traversal; list push-front, push-back and insert-in-middle; deque push-front, push-back and insert at a random position. Each timed loop also calls a std::mt19937 random-number function per operation.
claimed_speedup: No ratios are written in the repo; it publishes SVG graphs only. Values read from the plotted points of those SVGs at N = 122,880 (derived from page data, approximate): CcHashTable vs std::unordered_map insert about 10.2 ms vs 49.4 ms (4.8x), remove 6.8 ms vs 24.9 ms (3.7x), search 8.1 ms vs 16.6 ms (2.0x), iterator traversal 2.2 ms vs 3.2 ms (1.5x); CcTreeTable vs std::map insert 44.5 ms vs 85.9 ms (1.9x), search 45.4 ms vs 84.3 ms (1.9x), traversal equal; CcList vs std::list push-back 5.1 ms vs 12.5 ms (2.4x), push-front 5.2 ms vs 12.3 ms (2.4x), insert-middle 5.8 ms vs 12.4 ms (2.2x); CcDeque vs std::deque push-back 4.6 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.3x), push-front 4.1 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.5x), random-position insert 337 ms vs 2560 ms (7.6x). CcTreeTable lookups are slower than std::unordered_map at large N (about 45 ms vs 17 ms for search), and glib's GHashTable beats CcHashTable on traversal and search.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. CMakeLists.txt defines Release flags '-O3 -flto -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti' (C: '-O3 -flto'), but run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so those flags apply only if the author passed Release by hand. Google Benchmark v1.5.0, glib 2.63.0, Collections-C pinned only to 'master' (late-2019 snapshot).
hardware: Quad-core Intel Core i7-7820HQ (3.9 GHz max), Linux 4.15.0-72-generic x86_64 (README 'Equipment' section)
tradeoffs: Generic containers store void* pointers (or sized variants), so there is no type safety and values need boxing or casting; the C library is LGPL-3.0 (library-linking terms apply). Insertion into CcHashTable and CcTreeTable needs a user hash and comparison function. Allocations use malloc per node like std::list and std::map.
caveats: Third-party but competing: the benchmark repo belongs to the author of the rival cdcontainers library, was last updated 2019-12-27, and its star count is not shown on the pages opened. Numbers exist only as matplotlib SVG graphs; the figures above were recovered from the SVG point positions. Compiler name and version are not stated and run.sh does not set a build type, so the optimisation level is unconfirmed (about 50 ns per std::deque push-back including the random call suggests an optimised build, but that is an inference). Every timed loop calls a mersenne-twister random function per operation, which dilutes the container difference for push-back/push-front. The std side stores int and the C side stores int cast to void*, with std::hash<int> as the C++ hash. Collections-C was built from an unpinned 'master' of December 2019 using the old unprefixed API (hashtable_add, deque_add_last); the library has since been renamed to the cc_ prefix, so the benchmark code does not match current master and the numbers predate later changes. No std::vector comparison exists. Tier capped at C because compiler and effective flags are unstated.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: oz123/awesome-c#Data Structures listing for Collections-C; evidence found with WebSearch query 'Collections-C srdja benchmark performance compared to glib OR uthash OR klib', which surfaced github.com/maksimandrianov/cdcontainers.benchmarks; README, run.sh, CMakeLists.txt, benchmark sources and the 10 SVG graphs were opened

verification.tier_reason: A competitor's benchmark repo (maksimandrianov/cdcontainers.benchmarks, 1 star) with public Google Benchmark code and a stated CPU (i7-7820HQ), but no compiler version and no effective optimisation level: run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..', so the Release flags in CMakeLists.txt are not applied as published. Numbers exist only as SVG plots; the record's values match the SVG coordinates at N=122,880.
verification.notes: SVG values re-derived from point coordinates and match the record (e.g., map insert CcHashTable 10.2 ms vs std::unordered_map 49.4 ms; deque random insert 337 ms vs 2560 ms). Main shortcoming: run.sh builds without a build type, and the absolute timings look like an unoptimised C++ baseline, so the ratios are untrustworthy; kept at C with the flaw documented. Metadata checked: LGPL-3.0-or-later (file headers), 3.0k stars, last commit 2026-05-12.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence for the headline rows: cdcontainers.benchmarks passes IsEquil (returns 1 on equal) as the Collections-C key_compare while Collections-C treats key_cmp == 0 as equal (same at 5355d2f and current), so the table keeps only about 42% of inserted keys, every timed search returns not-found and every timed remove frees nothing (modelled from the published code); the CcHashTable insert 4.8x, remove 3.7x, search 2.0x and traversal 1.5x rows time no-ops (MQF precedent). The remaining TreeTable, list and deque rows were built with no -O (plain cmake, -Wall -Werror only) and show at best parity. Other: POINTER_HASH rotl32(k2,33) is undefined behaviour on 64-bit; void*-only; LGPL-3.0.

name: Grouped SIMD Hash Table
workload: Single-threaded insert+lookup benchmark with uint64 key/value pairs at up to 2M elements (~80% load factor), including a per-operation (insert / lookup-hit / lookup-miss) breakdown at 1M elements, using SSE2 grouped-metadata probing vs ankerl::unordered_dense's Robin Hood table.
claimed_speedup: At 1M elements: lookup-hit 1.69x faster, lookup-miss 1.21x faster, but insert 0.72x (i.e. ~1.4x slower) than ankerl::unordered_dense. Total wall time roughly ties/edges out ankerl at 1M (71.9ms vs 72.3ms) and 2M (156.3ms vs 157.4ms) elements; ankerl wins clearly at 100k-500k sizes.
tradeoffs: No deletion support, no resizing (fixed capacity, must be pre-sized), SSE2/x86-64 only (no ARM/NEON port), and the insert path is slower than the SOTA baseline it targets -- it only wins on lookup-heavy workloads above ~500k-1M elements.
caveats: Does NOT compare against std::unordered_map at all -- only against martinus/unordered_dense, which is itself already on the KNOWN_LIST as a faster-than-std project, so this is a comparison between two already-fast alternatives, not evidence against the stdlib baseline directly. Result is a narrow/mixed win (loses on inserts, roughly ties on total time). No CPU model stated, capping the tier below A. The README credits an AI 'Deep Research' tool and includes research-log files (INSIGHTS.md, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md), suggesting an exploratory/automated project rather than a vetted, independently reviewed library; very new (~9 months) and low-adoption (50 stars).
found_via: gh search repos --topic hashmap --sort stars --limit 20, then gh search repos "hash table" "SIMD" --limit 20

verification.tier_reason: README #results numbers match exactly (1M: 72.3 vs 71.9 ms; 2M: 157.4 vs 156.3 ms; insert 0.72x, hit 1.69x, miss 1.21x), and benchmark_final_sota.cpp plus the g++ command are public. No CPU model is given, so C. The only comparison is against ankerl::unordered_dense, another third-party library. No std::unordered_map or other incumbent is compared anywhere in the repo.
verification.notes: Reject: the only baseline is ankerl::unordered_dense (itself on the known list), which is a third-party library rather than the stdlib/incumbent, and the 'win' is a sub-1% tie on total time. Metadata checks out (MIT, 50 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-23).

name: libsixel
workload: 100 sequential runs of the img2sixel command line (libsixel 1.10.5) encoding one 256x256 JPEG (Lenna) to Sixel, output to /dev/null, versus the same for chafa and sixrs.
claimed_speedup: img2sixel 1.10.5 1.64 s for 100 runs versus chafa 1.18.2 7.32 s (about 4.5x faster, derived from page data); sixrs 1.66 s (a tie with img2sixel). Output sizes: img2sixel 121,993 bytes, chafa 4,248,878 bytes, sixrs 59,220 bytes.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.93.1 for sixrs only; libsixel and chafa builds and flags not stated; commands: img2sixel -p 256 -w 256 -h 256 -E fast -S, chafa -f sixels --size 256x256 -c 256 --animate off
stars_or_usage: 2.9k stars; Sixel library behind img2sixel and used by many terminal tools
tradeoffs: C library with an autotools build and bindings for Python, Perl, PHP and Ruby; the main license is MIT with seven further licences for bundled components (stb_image and others), all permissive. Several image loaders and a long CVE fix list in 1.8.7 (use-after-free and integer overflows in GIF, PNG and encoder paths) mean untrusted inputs need care.
caveats: The only numbers found are in the README of the sixrs crate (a competing Rust Sixel encoder, crate created 2026-06-29, 102 downloads, no repository link on crates.io), described there as a quick smoke benchmark and 'workload-specific'. Each run is a separate process on a 256x256 image, so startup cost dominates; chafa writes a 35x larger output (different dithering, palette and compression), so the tools do different work; img2sixel was run with -E fast and -S (fast encode, no sixel size optimisation) while chafa ran with its defaults. CPU model, libsixel and chafa build flags and the repo for the harness are not given, so this stays tier C. libsixel's own README, NEWS, ChangeLog and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the project emphasises quality and compatibility. libsixel's own site and the man pages were not opened.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: seed record pass starting from https://github.com/saitoha/libsixel; WebSearch 'libsixel img2sixel benchmark encoding speed faster than ImageMagick chafa' surfaced the sixrs crate README

verification.tier_reason: The sixrs crate README (0.1.2, unchanged in 0.1.3) gives the exact commands and a shell loop (/usr/bin/time over 100 runs) with tool versions and macOS, but no CPU model and no build flags for img2sixel or chafa; it is a one-off smoke test by the author of an obscure competing crate (102 downloads, no public repo), not a well-known independent suite, so C.
verification.notes: Numbers verified verbatim (img2sixel 1.64 s, sixrs 1.66 s, chafa 7.32 s for 100 runs; output bytes as recorded); the 4.5x over chafa is derived from page data and is a tie with sixrs. Shortcomings to record: the benchmarked img2sixel 1.10.5 is the archived libsixel/libsixel fork's release, not saitoha's 1.8.7 line; startup-dominated per-process timing; non-equivalent options (chafa --size in cells, 35x larger output); the record's gloss of -S was wrong (it is --static); many 2026 memory-safety CVEs fixed in saitoha/libsixel 1.8.7. Metadata checked: MIT, 2.9k stars, last commit 2026-06-15, not archived.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the only numbers (sixrs README, img2sixel 1.64 s vs chafa 7.32 s per 100 runs) compare unequal work. chafa was run with --size 256x256, which counts terminal cells: chafa 1.18.2 maps the 256-px source to 256x128 cells of 10x20 px (or the probed cell size), about 2560x2560 px, roughly 100x img2sixel's 256x256 pixels, matching chafa's 35x larger output (read chafa.c, chicle-options.c, chafa-util.c, chafa-canvas.c at tag 1.18.2); chafa also probes the terminal every run with a 5 s timeout. Different-work precedent (stb-zip). Also: per-process startup-dominated timing, measured img2sixel 1.10.5 is the archived libsixel/libsixel fork (not the saitoha line), -E fast is the default auto path, lossy 15-bit colour cache, objects not thread-safe, many 2026 CVEs fixed only in saitoha 1.8.7.

name: Pairing Heap (priority-queue-testing benchmark suite)
workload: Randomized insert-delete (heap capacity c=1024) and Dijkstra's algorithm on the USA road network, from Larkin/Sen/Tarjan, 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues' (ALENEX 2014).
claimed_speedup: Randomized insert-delete, c=1024: pairing heap 1.00x (fastest) vs implicit-2 (plain binary heap) at 11.87x (i.e. binary heap took 11.87x longer). Dijkstra on USA road map: pairing 1.68x vs implicit-2 3.84x baseline time (~2.3x faster). Sorting: pairing 4.29x vs implicit-2 4.75x (modest win only).
hardware: Dell PowerEdge SC1435, dual AMD Opteron 2212 (dual-core, 2.0GHz, 64KB L1 / 1MB L2 per core), 8GB DDR2-667, Springdale/PUIAS Linux, kernel 2.6.32
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (GitHub mirror of the defunct code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing, the benchmark suite behind the ALENEX 2014 paper)
tradeoffs: Pairing heap's edge is workload-specific: it dominates on randomized insert-delete and Dijkstra but only modestly beats binary heap on plain sorting, and loses ground on some decrease-key-heavy patterns to other specialized heaps. Comparison is against the paper's own C99 'implicit-2' binary heap (algorithmically identical to std::priority_queue's array-based heap), not literally against libstdc++/libc++'s container.
caveats: 2014-era hardware (AMD Opteron 2212), gcc -O4 with no stated vectorization flags. Repo is an unmaintained auto-export of a shut-down Google Code project, no license file. Paper's headline finding is nuanced -- simple binary heaps remain competitive overall; pairing heap's big wins are specific to certain workloads.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: arXiv export API query -> arXiv:1403.0252 (Larkin, Sen, Tarjan) -> paper cites code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing -> gh search repositories "priority-queue-testing" found the GitHub mirror

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed paper (ALENEX 2014, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611973198.7, confirmed via Semantic Scholar). The code is public (driver/trace_driver.c, run_scripts/, Makefile with gcc -O4), and the Opteron 2212 hardware is stated. But the baseline is the authors' own C implicit binary/d-ary heaps, not std::priority_queue or any shipped library, so it is not an A-grade run against the named baseline.
verification.notes: The record's Dijkstra figure was wrong: it compared pairing 1.68 to explicit-2 (3.84), not implicit-2 (1.17), so the claimed ~2.3x Dijkstra win is actually a ~1.4x loss. The entry stays because the paper does show real pairing-heap wins on degenerate and large-heap workloads, but it is a research testbed, not a drop-in library. [orchestrator, user-approved 2026-09-24: rejected; the cited Dijkstra result is a ~1.4x loss vs the implicit binary heap, i.e. the std::priority_queue design]

name: seq::tiered_vector (seq library)
workload: Insertion/deletion of single elements in the middle of the container; project's own qualitative description, no fixed element type/size stated
claimed_speedup: "Several orders of magnitude faster" than std::deque for middle insertion/deletion; project also states sorting a tiered_vector is slower than sorting a std::deque, and iterator-based random access can be slightly slower
tradeoffs: Segmented/tiered layout trades away std::deque's simplicity; the docs themselves say it is explicitly slower than std::deque for sorting and can be slower for pure random-access iteration; interface mimics std::deque but is not a literal drop-in
caveats: "Several orders of magnitude" is a qualitative claim with no exact numbers, workload size, compiler, or CPU model given; no reproducible benchmark artifact with numbers was found for this specific claim; the library's own docs conclude 'you should always benchmark with your own use cases'
